sentences.text: Barapasaurus tagorei is the sole recognized species within this genus and is viewed as a versatile, general-purpose dinosaur.
Its body plan featured pillar-like limbs and a short torso, adaptations that enforced a strictly four-legged stance.
The name translates to 'large-legged lizard', combining Indian terms for size and limb with the Greek word for reptile.
The specific epithet tagorei commemorates the Bengali poet and artist Rabindranath Tagore.
Excavations to uncover these remains commenced during the centenary year of Rabindranath Tagore's birth.
All known skeletal material originates from a single site near Pochampally in central India, embedded in clay and sandstone layers.
Initial bones were unearthed in 1958, with the majority of specimens recovered in 1960 and 1961.
The animal possessed elongated neck vertebrae, a trait characteristic of later sauropods.
Estimates place the creature at roughly 14 meters in length, with a mass of about 7 tons.
Vertebral spines show early signs of hollowing, a structural modification likely intended to reduce weight.
The backbone was reinforced by hyposphene-hypantrum joints, and the pelvic girdle included an extra sacral vertebra for stability.
The presence of six left femurs suggests at least six individuals were present, leading researchers to propose a herd death.
Originally described in 1975 without a specific group assignment, it is now placed within the infraorder Sauropoda.
It was once grouped with Vulcanodon in the family Vulcanodontidae, but this family is now considered invalid; Barapasaurus belongs to the broader group Gravisauria.
Fossils generally date to the Early Jurassic, specifically the Sinemurian to Pliensbachian stages, roughly 184 to 200 million years ago.
